module_title: DNS, Route 53 and Hybrid Name Resolution
review_basis: Original SAP Module 05 slide WebPs 4–6 inspected individually; narration follows depicted arrows, decisions and DNS caveats.
part_title: VPC DNS Settings, Private Zones and Namespace Precedence

scenes.title: VPC DNS settings: know who the client asks
scenes.visual_overview: An EC2 instance gets DNS server settings through DHCP options, choosing AmazonProvidedDNS or custom resolvers.
visual_walkthrough: Identify VPC base plus two and 169.254.169.253
Separate AmazonProvidedDNS and Resolver inbound endpoint access
scenes.visual_example: An EC2 instance uses a custom corporate DNS server that lacks forwarding to AWS private zones.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Check the client DNS settings and VPC attributes before editing hosted-zone records.
scenes.narration: In this flow an EC2 instance needs to know which DNS server to ask. Start on the left with the instance, then follow the arrow to its DHCP option configuration. The top route leads to AmazonProvidedDNS, the VPC Resolver, accessible at the VPC base address plus two and at one six nine dot two five four dot one six nine dot two five three. The bottom route leads to custom DNS servers, which require deliberate forwarding of relevant AWS private namespaces. The four numbered lower boxes distinguish two settings. Enable DNS support controls Amazon DNS resolution in the VPC. Enable DNS hostnames affects assignment of eligible DNS hostnames and is also relevant to private hosted zone support. Both attributes should be enabled for the private DNS features shown. The last box warns that an on-premises DNS server should not simply query the VPC base-plus-two address remotely; a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint is the normal supported integration. Finally, the lower footer distinguishes Resolver traffic from ordinary traffic filtered by endpoint security groups. Troubleshoot what DNS server the client is actually using before modifying records.

scenes.title: Private hosted zones: association controls visibility
scenes.visual_overview: A private zone owned by account A is associated with VPC A and cross-account VPC B but not VPC C.
visual_walkthrough: Trace private zone association arrows to VPC A and B
Explain why unassociated VPC C does not see the zone
Trace on-premises DNS through inbound Resolver endpoint
Contrast DNS visibility with routed network connectivity
scenes.visual_example: A zone owner authorizes another account's VPC association without exposing the zone to all VPCs in that account.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Hosted zone visibility follows explicit associations, not mere peering or Transit Gateway attachments.
scenes.narration: The large left panel shows a private hosted zone named corp dot example dot com. Account A owns it and associates its own VPC A, while a cross-account association grants visibility to VPC B in account B. On the far right, VPC C belongs to the same second account but is not associated, so it does not automatically resolve this private zone through its VPC Resolver. Notice the dashed lines: these are associations, not traffic forwarding routes. The horizontal strip below shows another use case, corporate users who can forward queries to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint hosted in an appropriately associated VPC. The bottom cards describe direct cross-account authorization, supported sharing patterns and the need for the correct VPC DNS settings. Importantly, VPC peering or Transit Gateway connectivity alone does not associate a private hosted zone. And a hosted zone association does not create routing between application networks. Validate both the DNS answer and the network path before concluding the service is available.

scenes.title: Which DNS namespace wins?
scenes.visual_overview: Three side-by-side panels cover longest suffix private-zone matching, negative answers and forwarding-rule precedence.
visual_walkthrough: Distinguish NXDOMAIN and NODATA in matching private zones
Follow corp.example.com forwarding rule before same-domain private zone
Mention reverse PTR namespaces and auto-defined Resolver rules
scenes.visual_example: The query api.dev.example.com selects the associated dev.example.com zone, not a less-specific example.com zone.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Resolve namespace precedence and selected rules before changing records.
scenes.narration: This comparison is about which DNS configuration answers when more than one namespace could match. In the first panel, the VPC has both example dot com and the more specific dev dot example dot com private zones. A query for api dot dev dot example dot com uses the longer matching suffix. In the middle panel, suppose a selected private zone covers the question but lacks the requested name or record type. The response can be NXDOMAIN or NODATA, and Route 53 Resolver does not automatically fall back to public DNS for that name. The third panel introduces a different precedence rule: a Resolver forwarding rule that matches the exact same domain as a private hosted zone takes priority, sending the request toward its configured target DNS servers. The lower strip adds reverse DNS namespaces, including in-addr dot arpa and ip six dot arpa, which can interact with automatically defined Resolver rules. For a production incident, inspect VPC zone associations, the most specific suffix and forwarding rules in that order. Creating another record is pointless if the query is being answered or forwarded by an entirely different namespace.
